growth_story.headline: With no growth record in the data, sources describe a North Korean economy held down by sanctions and state control, now leaning on Russia.
growth_story.arc: The data file holds no income per person figures for North Korea, so it shows no eras and no 10-year average for 2016 to 2025. The sources warn that the country publishes almost no economic statistics, and that outside estimates show the direction of growth rather than its size. On their telling, fast industrial growth faded after the mid-1960s, and trend growth turned negative once Soviet support ended and trade with China moved onto commercial terms. Markets spread after 2000, but tighter sanctions brought sharp falls in output in 2017 and 2018, and the border closure from 2020 deepened the slump. The sources describe a rebound in 2023 and 2024, helped by trade with China and Russia, while the state has pulled markets and foreign currency back under its control.

threads.title: Decline after Soviet support ended
threads.text: Fast post-war industrial growth faded after the mid-1960s. Growth then slowed and turned negative as Soviet support ended and China put trade on commercial terms. The OECD reported in 2020 that output was reportedly below its 1990 level, even though the population had grown.

citations.title: North Korea: The last transition economy? (OECD Economics Department Working Papers No. 1607)

threads.title: Sanctions and the border closure
threads.text: Tighter international sanctions brought sharp falls in output in 2017 and 2018. The border closure from 2020 then blocked trade and movement. The OECD says sanctions still restrict formal trade, finance and investment.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Korea 2024
citations.quote: after severely contracting in 2017 and 2018 as a result of tightened international sanctions

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Korea 2024
citations.quote: blocking human and material exchanges across the border and restricting domestic movement, at considerable economic cost

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Korea 2026
citations.quote: International sanctions continue to restrict formal trade, finance and investment.

threads.title: Markets grow, then retreat
threads.text: Market trading spread after 2000, as part of a shift to a hybrid system that mixed state control with private initiative. Since the pandemic the state has tightened its grip again, curbing informal markets, enterprise freedom and the use of foreign currency.

citations.title: North Korea: The last transition economy? (OECD Economics Department Working Papers No. 1607)
citations.quote: the scale and breadth of market activities has visibly expanded since the turn of the millennium, as part of a transition to a hybrid system

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Korea 2024
citations.quote: North Korean authorities tightened state control over markets and external trade during the pandemic and seem determined to maintain control going forward

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Korea 2026
citations.quote: the suppression of jangmadang activity (informal market), the rollback of limited enterprise autonomy and the re-centralisation of price setting

threads.title: A turn towards Russia
threads.text: Trade with China has recovered since 2022 but stays well below its level before 2018. Ties with Russia have grown fast since 2023, bringing trade, food and foreign currency linked to military cooperation.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Korea 2026
citations.quote: Trade with China rebounded strongly since 2022, although volumes remain well below pre-2018 levels following China's compliance with international sanctions.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Korea 2026
citations.quote: Increased trade, food supplies and unreported revenue streams linked to military cooperation have helped alleviate shortages and improve foreign-exchange availability.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Korea 2024
citations.quote: Trade between North Korea and Russia is also suspected to have expanded since the North Korea - Russia summit in September 2023.

threads.title: Power, food and materials short
threads.text: Factories run shorter hours because power and raw materials are scarce, and food shortages were severe from 2020 to 2022. The OECD doubts that factories built under a plan launched in 2024 can run as planned, given chronic shortages and the priority given to military production.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Korea 2024
citations.quote: manufacturing sectors are running at shorter hours due to intensifying power shortages and difficulties in securing raw materials

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Korea 2024
citations.quote: North Korea is thought to have suffered severe food shortages from 2020 to 2022 due to border closures and failing crops.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Korea 2026
citations.quote: Chronic shortages of electricity, raw materials and skilled labour, combined with the prioritisation of military production, raise questions about whether newly built facilities can operate

since_last_year.text: The OECD's July 2026 survey of Korea reports that North Korea's economy grew faster in 2024 than in 2023, led by manufacturing, mining and building. It also reports that the North Korean won lost much of its value from 2024, as the state raised official wages while tightening control of markets and foreign exchange.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Korea 2026
citations.quote: North Korea’s economy accelerated in 2024, growing by 3.7% (following growth of +3.1% in 2023 and -0.2% in 2022), its fastest pace in eight years

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Korea 2026
citations.quote: After a decade of relative stability, the North Korean Won (KPW) depreciated sharply in 2024

growth_story.tension: The sources report a rebound in 2023 and 2024, but the data file holds no income per person figures to check it against, and the OECD itself says outside estimates show the direction of growth rather than its size. The OECD also reported in 2020 that output was below its 1990 level while the population had grown, which would leave income per person lower still, but the data cannot confirm this.
